Mela Muter, born Maria Melania Mutermilch, was a Polish-Jewish artist who settled in Paris in 1901 and became a distinctive figure within the École de Paris. Her expressive, psychologically charged portraits combined a Slavic sensibility with the cosmopolitan culture of her adopted home. In Le sculpteur François Pompon dans son atelier, this sensitivity is directed towards a fellow artist, whom she depicts absorbed in thought within his studio. Seen from just inside the doorway, Pompon sits at a modest table, while a pristine white cockerel, Coq, 1914, rests on a stool before him. A hammer suggests a work in progress, while the sculptures surrounding him provide an intimate insight into his practice.

Muter's earthy palette of ochres, browns, deep reds and soft whites conveys the warmth of the atelier, enlivened by bold contours and assured brushwork. The simplified animal sculptures anticipate the essentialist language for which Pompon became renowned. Trained under Pierre Louis Rouillard and later working in Auguste Rodin's studio, Pompon devoted himself exclusively to animals after 1905, seeking, in his own words, 'the essential'. The work was formerly in the collection of Gérald Schurr, the French critic and collector whose celebrated collection of portraits of artists and writers included the present work in his Portraits et Autoportraits, published in connection with an exhibition in Neuilly-sur-Seine in 1986. Here, Muter captures not simply the sculptor, but the quiet concentration and solitude of artistic creation.

Beautifully executed in pencil and coloured crayon, Nude Boy captures David Hockney at an exciting moment when both his surroundings and his vision were beginning to change. Dating from 1966, the drawing belongs to Hockney's third year in Los Angeles, following his move from London in 1964. The brilliant light and open spaces of Southern California offered a striking contrast to the muted greys of London, and with this new environment came a new visual language. One in which the male figure could be observed with an increasing sense of freedom, intimacy and ease.

Here, a young man reclines at ease, his body loosely described in soft, swiftly applied strokes of coloured crayon. The flashes of vivid green lend the drawing a particular freshness, their unexpected intensity animating the otherwise delicate composition and heightening the impression of a scene caught in the immediacy of the moment. The informality of the pose and the spontaneity of the handling give the drawing a quality of fleeting observation, as though Hockney has captured the figure in an unguarded moment. Rather than relying on the literary references and graphic shorthand that had characterised much of his early work, he observes the body with an openness that feels distinctly Californian. This new frankness was significant. In England, where sexual relations between men remained illegal until 1967, Hockney had often encoded homoerotic subjects through wit, quotation and symbolism. In Los Angeles, his male figures could increasingly be presented with a directness that was both tender and unapologetic.

Nude Boy thus belongs to a moment of both personal and artistic liberation. It was in 1966, the year of execution of the present work, that Hockney met Peter Schlesinger, who would become his lover, model and muse, and whose presence would profoundly shape his figurative work throughout the following years. With its loose lines, sunlit palette and unselfconscious pose, the drawing has the freshness of an artist looking at the world anew. Nude Boy marks the emergence of a more intimate and liberated approach to the male figure that would become central to Hockney's work in Los Angeles.

Against an expanse of deep, enveloping darkness, a poised figure emerges in Alex Katz's characteristically incisive style. In Bill, the effect is particularly striking: the warmly illuminated face appears to hover against the black ground, as though momentarily caught in the glare of a stage light. Intimate yet cinematic, the composition transforms an otherwise quiet moment of observation into an image charged with atmosphere and presence. Katz's reduction of the surrounding environment to an almost absolute field of darkness heightens the immediacy of the sitter, directing the viewer's attention towards the subtle modelling of the face and the distinctive economy of the artist's touch. Nothing distracts from the encounter; the figure occupies the picture plane with an almost theatrical clarity.

Katz developed his distinctive language of figuration in deliberate opposition to the prevailing dominance of Abstract Expressionism in post-war New York. Having studied at Cooper Union during the height of the movement, he sought to endow figurative painting with the same scale, immediacy and visual authority as the monumental canvases of Willem de Kooning and Franz Kline. Rather than rejecting the lessons of abstraction, however, Katz absorbed its formal radicalism, translating its emphasis on scale, surface and immediacy into a new mode of portraiture. Bill embodies this ambition in its expansive, widescreen format, which lends the portrait an imposing physical presence, while its pared-back composition retains the cool, assured economy that became Katz's hallmark. The figure is neither surrounded by narrative detail nor situated within a recognisable interior; instead, Katz isolates his subject and allows the act of looking itself to become the principal subject of the painting.

Painted in 2000, the present work belongs to Katz's celebrated series of Black Paintings, in which darkness becomes not merely a background but an active pictorial element. The 'black' of these works is never absolute; Katz modulates its depth and tonal character, creating a richly atmospheric field from which his sitters appear to surface. This subtle manipulation of the ground is fundamental to the visual drama of the series: rather than functioning as a neutral void, the darkness possesses its own presence, absorbing and simultaneously amplifying the figure before it. Against this enveloping ground, colour acquires an almost luminous intensity. Warm ochres and oranges animate the face, while discreet accents of blue and pink recall Katz's sustained engagement with the bold chromatic vocabulary and reductive forms of Pop and Minimalism. The palette is highly selective, allowing each colour to assume maximum visual impact without compromising the restraint of the overall composition.

The resulting tension between apparent simplicity and exacting construction is central to the power of the work. Katz's paintings often possess the immediacy of an image registered in an instant, yet this apparent spontaneity is underpinned by an extraordinary sensitivity to proportion, contour and colour. The edges of the figure are sharply articulated, while the simplified planes of the face retain just enough information to establish both character and presence. His economy is therefore not one of reduction for its own sake, but of precision: extraneous detail is removed so that what remains carries greater weight. Every element is deliberate, yet nothing feels laboured; the image retains the effortless clarity of a fleeting visual encounter.

Throughout his career, Katz transformed those closest to him into enigmatic presences that are at once immediately recognisable and rigorously distilled. Familiarity, however, never diminished the sense of discovery inherent in the act of painting. As Katz himself observed, 'The thing of appearances to me, what a thing appears to be, is like always a mystery and it's like a brand-new situation' (Alex Katz, quoted in 'Oral history interview with Alex Katz', Smithsonian, Archives of American Art, 20 October 1969). This idea of appearance as a continual process of discovery is particularly resonant in Bill, where recognition is balanced against a deliberate withholding of information. We are given the face, but not the circumstances surrounding it; the sitter is present with remarkable immediacy yet remains psychologically elusive.

Katz's distinctive synthesis of observation and abstraction drew upon a wide range of sources, from the graphic economy of Paul Klee and the modernist poise of Édouard Manet and Henri Matisse to the saturated colour and simplified forms of contemporary popular imagery. His engagement with these traditions was never merely referential. Instead, he distilled their formal principles into a visual language capable of capturing the particularities of modern life with remarkable economy. In this respect, Katz's portraits occupy a fascinating position between the personal and the impersonal: they are rooted in specific individuals, yet rendered through a vocabulary of simplified contours, emphatic colour and flattened space that gives them an almost archetypal quality. The sitter becomes at once a person and an image.

With its commanding scale, saturated colour and enveloping darkness, Billexemplifies Katz's singular ability to invest the everyday with an enduring sense of presence. The figure is held in a state of quiet suspension, while the surrounding void introduces an element of ambiguity and tension. There is a distinctly cinematic quality to the encounter: the sitter appears to emerge from the darkness, momentarily illuminated and fully present, before seeming to recede once more into the black. The painting consequently occupies a space between appearance and disappearance, presence and absence. Its drama lies not in gesture or narrative, but in the sustained intensity of looking. It is precisely this tension between immediacy and mystery, recognition and abstraction, that gives Katz's portraiture its enduring power.

"Sculpture is like a caress. You touch the form, you can give the forms the softness, the sensuality you want. It's magnificent." - Fernando Botero

Executed in 1988, Ballerina belongs to a significant period in Fernando Botero's sculptural practice, when the artist had fully established his distinctive language of exaggerated volume and was exploring the expressive possibilities of the human figure in the third dimension. The female nude was a central subject throughout Botero's career, providing an enduring means through which to investigate sensuality, proportion and form. In the present work, the artist turns to the ballerina, traditionally associated with delicacy, grace and weightlessness, and recasts her within the monumental, voluptuous vocabulary that had become synonymous with his art. 

Botero's fascination with volume was rooted in his engagement with the history of Western art. During his formative years in Europe, particularly in Italy, he studied the masters of the Renaissance, whose emphasis on volume and the physicality of the human figure had a lasting impact on his practice. His encounter with European art, particularly during his years studying in Florence, led him to engage deeply with a tradition of voluptuous nudes and statuesque figures, which would become an important foundation for his own sculptural language. Botero himself spoke of his interest in the 'manifestation of volume in art' (Fernando Botero quoted in 'An Interview with Fernando Botero', in Museum of Latin American Art, Long Beach, 5 September 2023), recognising in artists including Giotto, Masaccio, Piero della Francesca, Michelangelo and Raphael the potential of volume to heighten sensuality and form. The female nude, with its long and distinguished place within the Western canon, therefore offered Botero an ideal subject through which to develop his own highly individual conception of the body.

The ballerina brings another dimension to this investigation. Dance is concerned with balance, rhythm and the controlled movement of the body through space. In Ballerina, Botero creates a striking tension between the physical demands of the pose and the apparent ease of the dancer. With her arms extended and one leg dramatically raised while the other balances en pointe, the figure appears suspended in a moment of extraordinary poise, her expansive limbs describing an elegant arc through space as her substantial, rounded body resists conventional associations between ballet and physical fragility, transforming the movement of dance into a solid and enduring sculptural presence. Rather than diminishing the body to suggest grace, Botero makes its volume the very source of the sculpture's presence. The result is a dancer who appears both grounded and buoyant, her pose conveying the discipline and elegance of ballet through an unmistakably Botero-esque physicality.

This treatment of the female body reflects Botero's broader approach to the nude. He returned repeatedly to reclining, seated and standing women throughout his career, using the figure not as a portrait of an individual but as a vehicle for exploring form. His avoidance of specific physical characteristics allowed his figures to function as types rather than portraits, emphasising their sculptural qualities over individual identity. In Ballerina, this approach transforms the dancer into an archetypal figure, one that is recognisable through her pose and gesture, yet ultimately defined by the rhythm of her contours and the sensuality of her volume. The sculpture demonstrates how Botero could take a familiar subject from European artistic tradition and make it distinctly his own. 

Ballerina is also characteristic of Botero's mature engagement with sculpture during the 1980s. After returning to sculpture in 1973, he increasingly explored the possibilities offered by bronze, a medium that allowed him to realise the substantial volumes of his paintings and drawings as physical objects. By the later 1980s, sculpture had become an increasingly prominent aspect of his international practice. His 1987 retrospective at the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, brought together his work across these mediums and demonstrated the continuity of his subjects and forms. Ballerina, executed only a year later, belongs to this mature period, when Botero's sculptural language had achieved both confidence and international recognition. 

Ballerina brings together many of Botero's most enduring concerns: the female nude, the sensuality of volume, the legacy of European art and the expressive potential of sculpture; while the contradiction between the ballerina's disciplined pose and her monumental physicality transforms a familiar symbol of grace into a powerful study of form. In this way, Botero's treatment of the ballerina exemplifies his ability to reinterpret established subjects through his highly individual language, balancing monumentality with grace and sensuality with restraint.

"I don't paint apples anymore. Oranges and bananas are the authentic fruits of the tropic. Apples are for snobs." - Fernando Botero

Against a deep brown background, a group of oranges is gathered upon a draped table, their rounded forms set against the folds of the cloth, while a knife rests quietly amongst the fruit. Painted in 1989, Still Life with Oranges is a striking still life that brings together Fernando Botero's enduring preoccupation with volume, colour and the transformation of everyday subjects. In the present work, the familiar conventions of the still life become a vehicle for Botero's distinctive exploration of form and colour, transforming a familiar subject through a distinctive visual language that came to define his work. 

Still life occupied an important position within Botero's practice, offering him an especially direct means of investigating the fundamental principles of his art. As Botero himself observed, 'everything you see is an excuse to paint', (Fernando Botero quoted in 'An Interview with Fernando Botero', in Museum of Latin American Art, Long Beach, 5 September 2023) and his still lifes demonstrate precisely this attitude towards the visual world. They also place his work within the long tradition of European still-life painting, a genre to which he repeatedly returned while reinterpreting its conventions through his own visual language. The artist's still lifes have been associated with the concentrated compositions of seventeenth-century Spanish painting, in which a limited number of objects are isolated against dark backgrounds and imbued with a quiet, almost ceremonial presence. Botero draws on this tradition while subjecting it to his own sensibility; the objects become fuller, rounder and more emphatic, while intense colour and deliberate simplification establish an unmistakably modern visual language.

The orange in particular, held a particular fascination for Botero. In a 1994 conversation with the writer Carlos Fuentes, the artist described the orange as 'a sphere' and 'the most simple and perfect form', while also expressing his affinity with its intense colour (Fernando Botero quoted in Carlos Fuentes, Latin American Artists in Their Studios, New York, 1994, pp. 40). For Botero, the challenge lay in taking an object so familiar and making it distinctly personal – he described this as the 'orange test' or 'fire test of painting' (Carlos Fuentes, ibid., p. 44). Artists throughout history had painted oranges, but the individual treatment of the fruit revealed the particular language of the painter. The present work offers a compelling illustration of this principle, with the orange becoming a vehicle for Botero's exploration of form, colour and proportion.

The late 1980s saw Botero confidently revisiting many of the subjects that had occupied him throughout his career. These recurring motifs were not simply repetitions, but offered continual opportunities to reconsider the possibilities of form, colour and composition. In Still Life with Oranges, this process is particularly evident in the way a simple arrangement of fruit becomes an exercise in volume and pictorial balance. The fruit provides an ideal subject for Botero's investigation of volume. Throughout his career, he sought for the 'sensuality of form', an approach rooted in his admiration for the tactile qualities of Renaissance painting. In Still Life with Oranges, the fruit is not simply represented as botanical fact but transformed into solid, self-contained forms that occupy the canvas with considerable presence. The orange thus becomes more than a subject to be depicted: it becomes a means through which Botero explores the physical presence of painted form.

Colour is equally fundamental. The saturated orange tones of the fruit form the visual centre of the composition, glowing against the rich brown background. Rather than relying upon complex perspectival space, Botero creates depth through the contrast between these areas of colour and the subtle modulation of the oranges themselves. The intensity of the fruit is tempered by the softer pink of the tablecloth and deep brown ground, creating the sense of 'quiet colour' that Botero valued, in which contrasting tones remain harmonious rather than competing for attention. Despite the intensity of the oranges, this carefully controlled palette lends the painting a sense of stillness, allowing its vivid colour to remain striking without overwhelming the composition.

The other elements of the composition reinforce its informal, almost spontaneous quality. The pink tablecloth introduces a soft counterpoint to the richness of the fruit, its loose draping suggesting a scene captured in an unguarded moment. The knife, meanwhile, introduces a slender, linear element into an otherwise predominantly organic arrangement. The fruit, tablecloth and knife are unified through Botero's consistent treatment of form and colour, each rendered according to the same visual language. As Botero observed, when the fruit, table, napkin and utensils are treated in this way, 'everything is rendered in the same fashion, therefore the whole work radiates a sense of unity, harmony, and coherence' (Fernando Botero quoted in John Sillevis, The Baroque World of Fernando Botero, Virginia, 2006, p. 27).

In Still Life with Oranges, Botero takes one of the simplest subjects in the history of still-life painting and makes it a highly individual statement. The fruit, tablecloth and knife are stripped of unnecessary detail, allowing colour, proportion and the physical presence of each object to carry the composition. Yet it is the oranges themselves that remain most striking – they are transformed through Botero's treatment of volume and colour into a distinctive expression of his artistic vision. The painting therefore offers a compelling answer to Botero's own 'orange test', demonstrating how an object painted countless times before could, through the particularities of his hand, become unquestionably Botero.
